title: Cap. III open + Rat. 1: common inefficacious will before foresight of merits
latin:
CAP. III. Argumenta adversariorum expenduntur & dissolvuntur.

Jam rationes adversariorum ventilemus. Primo igitur conantur demonstrare, neminem esse efficaci Dei voluntate electum ad gloriam nisi ex meritis praevisis, hujusmodi argumentatione:

Rat. 1. Voluntas dandi vitam aeternam, quae antecedit praevisionem meritorum, est quaedam voluntas communis & inefficax, quae ex aequo respicit omnes homines, tam praeteritos quam praedestinatos: Ergo quod vult Deus alicui efficaciter dare gloriam, pendet ex praevisione meritorum.
pass_a:
Chapter III. The adversaries' arguments are weighed and dissolved.

Now let us ventilate the adversaries' reasons. First, therefore, they try to demonstrate that no one is elected to glory by an efficacious will of God except from foreseen merits, by this kind of argumentation:

Reason 1. The will of giving eternal life which precedes the foresight of merits is a certain common and inefficacious will, which regards all men equally, both the reprobate and the predestinate: Therefore, that God efficaciously wills to give glory to someone depends on the foresight of merits.
pass_b:
Cap. III — the adversaries' arguments weighed and answered.

Now to their reasons. First they try to prove no one is chosen for glory by God's efficacious will except from foreseen merits, like this:

Rat. 1. The will to give eternal life that comes before foresight of merits is only a common, inefficacious will, looking equally at all — reprobate and predestinate alike. So if God efficaciously wills glory for someone, that hangs on foresight of merits.

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1: Bannes — common will only before sin / Adam intact
latin: Rej. Communis illa voluntas dandi vitam aeternam omnibus, (ut optime Bannes) secundum nostrum modum intelligendi concipitur ante praescientiam peccati. Eo igitur tantum valebit, ut inde probetur, Deum in Adamo integro voluisse communem omnium hominum salutem, atque in hunc finem dedisse Adamo sufficientia media, quibus si uti voluisset, neque seipsum, neque posteros in aeternae mortis reatum praecipitasset. Posito autem primi Adami lapsu, nego Deum unquam habuisse communem & indifferentem illam voluntatem dandi omnibus vitam aeternam in Christo Jesu.
pass_a: Rejection. That common will of giving eternal life to all (as Bannes excellently) is conceived, according to our mode of understanding, before the foreknowledge of sin. Therefore it will avail only so far that from it it is proved that God in Adam intact willed the common salvation of all men, and to this end gave Adam sufficient means which, if he had willed to use them, he would have precipitated neither himself nor his posterity into the guilt of eternal death. But the fall of the first Adam having been posited, I deny that God ever had that common and indifferent will of giving eternal life to all in Christ Jesus.
pass_b: Rejection. That "common will to give eternal life to all" (Bannes is right) is only how we picture things before foreknowledge of sin. It proves at most that in intact Adam God willed everyone's salvation and gave him enough means — if Adam had used them, neither he nor his line would have fallen into eternal death's guilt. Once Adam fell, I deny God ever had a common, indifferent will to give eternal life to all in Christ Jesus.

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1: reprobates only under 'if they will' — not equal termini
latin: Quoad reprobandos, non habuit voluntatem quae proxime referebatur ad eorum salutem: nam qui id defendunt, coguntur hoc additamentum apponere, Si ipsi voluerint. Cum ergo Deus praevideat hoc ipsorum Nolle, & nolit illis dare id, quod revera dat electis, manifestum est hanc voluntatem Dei non ex aequo terminari ad salutem electorum & non-electorum.
pass_a: As for those to be reprobated, he did not have a will that referred proximately to their salvation: for those who defend that are forced to add this rider, If they themselves have willed. Since therefore God foresees this their Not-willing, and does not will to give them that which he really gives to the elect, it is manifest that this will of God is not terminated equally to the salvation of the elect and of the non-elect.
pass_b: Toward the reprobate he had no will aimed next at their salvation: defenders must tack on "if they themselves will." Since God foresees their Not-willing and will not give them what he really gives the elect, that will clearly does not terminate equally on elect and non-elect salvation.

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1: sufficient aids fail for pagans/infants — Augustine De nat.
latin: Porro, qui Deo tribuunt hanc voluntatem beneplaciti circa omnium salutem, id inde colligunt, quod omnibus det sufficientia auxilia ad salutem obtinendam: quod tamen nec de Paganis, quibus Christi nomen & Evangelii lumen nunquam innotuit, nec de infantibus illorum qui absque baptismo moriuntur, (ut de aliis nihil dicam) unquam probabunt. Augustinus diserte docet, damnari multos qui justificari & salvari non potuerint, De Nat. & grat. cap. 8. & 9.
pass_a: Further, those who attribute to God this will of good pleasure concerning the salvation of all gather it from this, that he gives to all sufficient helps for obtaining salvation: which yet they will never prove either of the Pagans, to whom the name of Christ and the light of the Gospel never became known, or of their infants who die without baptism (to say nothing of others). Augustine expressly teaches that many are damned who could not be justified and saved, On Nature and Grace, chapters 8 and 9.
pass_b: Those who put on God a good-pleasure will for everyone's salvation infer it from "sufficient helps for all" — yet they never prove that of pagans who never heard Christ's name or Gospel light, nor of their infants dying unbaptized (never mind the rest). Augustine says plainly many are damned who could not be justified and saved (On Nature and Grace 8–9).

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1: Augustine Ep. 107 / 1 Tim. 2:4 — God not willing all alike
latin: Et Epist. 107. inter duodecim sententias quae ad fidem rectam & catholicam pertinere affirmat, haec quarta est, Scimus gratiam non omnibus hominibus dari, & quibus datur, non solum secundum merita operum non dari, sed nec secundum merita voluntatis eorum quibus datur: quod maxime apparet in parvulis. Et non multo post, hanc ipsam objectionem respiciens, quae obtendi solet de voluntate communi & indifferenti quoad salutem omnium, haec verba adjungit, recitatione nostra & observatione vestra dignissima: Manifestum est eos qui huic resistunt tam perspicuae veritati, non intelligere omnino qua locutione sit dictum, quod omnes homines vult Deus salvos fieri, cum tam multi salvi non fiant. Non quia ipsi, sed quia Deus non vult: quod sine ulla caligine manifestatur in parvulis. Quod igitur dictum est, OMNES HOMINES VULT DEUS SALVOS FIERI, cum tam multos nolit salvos fieri, ideo dictum est, quia omnes qui salvi fiunt, nisi ipse velit non fiunt; & si quae alio modo intelligi possunt, ut tamen huic apertissimae veritati, in qua vides tam multos, volentibus hominibus, sed Deo nolente, salvos non fieri, contraria esse non possunt. Hactenus Augustinus.
pass_a: And in Epistle 107, among twelve sentences which he affirms pertain to right and catholic faith, this is the fourth: We know that grace is not given to all men, and to those to whom it is given, it is given not only not according to the merits of works, but not even according to the merits of the will of those to whom it is given: which appears most of all in little ones. And not much later, regarding this very objection which is customarily urged about a common and indifferent will as to the salvation of all, he adds these words, most worthy of our recital and your observation: It is manifest that those who resist this so clear truth do not understand at all in what manner of speaking it was said that God wills all men to be saved, when so many are not saved. Not because they [will not], but because God does not will: which is manifested without any darkness in little ones. What therefore was said, GOD WILLS ALL MEN TO BE SAVED, when he does not will so many to be saved, was said for this reason, because all who are saved are not saved unless he himself wills; and if any things can be understood in another way, yet they cannot be contrary to this most open truth, in which you see that so many, with men willing, but God not willing, are not saved. Thus far Augustine.
pass_b: Epistle 107's fourth of twelve catholic sentences: we know grace is not given to all; and where it is given, not by works' merits, nor even by the will's merits of those who get it — clearest in infants. Soon after, on the usual "common indifferent will to save all" objection, he adds words worth quoting: those who fight this plain truth miss how "God wills all to be saved" is said when so many are not. Not because they refuse, but because God does not will — obvious in infants. So "GOD WILLS ALL MEN TO BE SAVED," though he does not will so many saved, means all who are saved are saved only if he wills; any other reading must not contradict that open truth: many are not saved though men will it, if God does not. So Augustine.

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1: Vasquez infants — deny invented common good-pleasure will
latin: Ipse Vasques ante rei evidentiam coactus, concedit nobis, quibusdam parvulis nec sufficiens remedium per Christum humana diligentia potuisse applicari. Ego addo, nec Divina providentia fuisse applicatum. Atque hinc a posteriori colligimus, Deum non habuisse hanc communem, quam comminiscuntur, salvandi omnes & singulos beneplaciti voluntatem. Postremo, quod maxime facit ad argumentationis propositae nervos incidendos, nego illam Dei voluntatem, quae ante praescientiam meritorum decrevit dare vitam aeternam electis, fuisse solummodo hanc communem, inefficacem, & quam vocant, simplicis affectus sive complacentiae; atque affirmo fuisse specialem quandam & efficacissimam voluntatem.
pass_a: Vasquez himself, forced before the evidence of the matter, grants us that to certain little ones not even a sufficient remedy through Christ could have been applied by human diligence. I add, nor was it applied by Divine providence. And hence from the posterior we gather that God did not have this common will of good pleasure of saving all and each which they invent. Finally, what most of all cuts the nerves of the proposed argumentation: I deny that that will of God which before the foreknowledge of merits decreed to give eternal life to the elect was only this common, inefficacious [will], and what they call [a will] of simple affection or complacency; and I affirm that it was a certain special and most efficacious will.
pass_b: Even Vasquez, pressed by the facts, grants that for some infants no sufficient Christ-remedy could be applied by human care. I add: nor was it applied by divine providence. So a posteriori God never had that invented common good-pleasure will to save every single person. Finally — and this most cuts their argument's nerve — I deny that the will by which God, before foreknowledge of merits, decreed eternal life for the elect was only that common, inefficacious "simple affection / complacency" will; I affirm it was a special, most efficacious will.

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1 close: electing will causes merits — sum before Rat. 2
latin: Hoc ex eo liquet, quia haec ipsa gratuita voluntas Dei, quae praecedit merita sive bona opera nostra, est causa horum meritorum: Quomodo igitur dicamus illam Dei voluntatem quae meritis praesupponitur esse communem, aequalem & indifferentem quoad omnes, cum in aliquibus efficiat haec ipsa quae vocantur merita, in aliis non efficiat? Manifestum apparet discrimen in effectu; ergo intelligitur etiam in ipsa causa. Audiamus iterum (quem nunquam satis audire possumus) loquentem Augustinum: Vera Dei gratia est, quae non secundum merita nostra datur, sed quae dat merita ipsa cum datur, quia praevenit hominis voluntatem bonam, nec eam cujusquam invenit in corde, sed facit. Sic itaque haec summa responsionis nostrae: Non esse aequalem aut indifferentem de omnium salute illam Dei voluntatem, quae antecedit praescientiam bonorum operum, quandoquidem in aliquibus vult Deus producere haec opera gratiae, quae ducant ad gloriam, in aliis non vult: Male ergo inferunt, ex praevisione meritorum incipere efficacem Dei voluntatem de danda salute electis, cum ea manifeste se exerat in illa voluntate dandi haec ipsa merita, quae voluntas praevisionem meritorum praecessit, atque ad salutem haec ipsa illorum merita ordinavit.
pass_a: This is clear from this, because this very gratuitous will of God which precedes our merits or good works is the cause of these merits: How then shall we say that that will of God which is presupposed to merits is common, equal, and indifferent as to all, when in some it effects these very things which are called merits, in others it does not effect them? A distinction appears manifest in the effect; therefore it is understood also in the cause itself. Let us hear again Augustine speaking (whom we can never hear enough): True grace of God is that which is not given according to our merits, but which gives the merits themselves when it is given, because it precedes man's good will, and does not find it in anyone's heart, but makes it. Thus therefore this is the sum of our response: That will of God which precedes the foreknowledge of good works is not equal or indifferent concerning the salvation of all, seeing that in some God wills to produce these works of grace which lead to glory, in others he does not will: Therefore they badly infer that the efficacious will of God concerning giving salvation to the elect begins from the foresight of merits, when that [will] manifestly puts itself forth in that will of giving these very merits, which will preceded the foresight of merits, and ordained these very merits of theirs to salvation.
pass_b: Clear why: that free will of God before our merits or good works is itself their cause. How then call the will presupposed to merits common, equal, and indifferent to all, when in some it effects those "merits" and in others not? Effect differs; so does the cause. Hear Augustine again (never enough): true grace is not given by our merits but gives the merits when given — it goes before a good will, finds it in no heart, and makes it. Sum of our answer: the divine will before foresight of good works is not equal or indifferent about everyone's salvation, since in some God wills grace-works that lead to glory and in others he does not. So they wrongly start the efficacious saving will for the elect from foresight of merits — that will already shows itself in willing to give those merits, which will came before merit-foresight and ordered those merits to salvation.
